# Sexual dysfunction and paraphilic disorders

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Obstetrics/gynecology > Sexuality and sexual development disorders > Sexual dysfunction and paraphilic disorders*

[Original Article Link](/library/to0XdS)

---

## Summary

<u>Sexual dysfunctions</u> are conditions characterized by clinically significant difficulty in experiencing sexual pleasure (e.g., <u>genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder</u>) or responding to sexual stimuli (e.g., <u>erectile disorder</u>, <u>premature ejaculation</u>). Diagnosis is made using <u>DSM-5</u> diagnostic criteria. Diagnosis requires exclusion of organic causes, such as <u>dyspareunia in women</u> and <u>erectile dysfunction</u>, both of which are detailed separately. Management of <u>sexual dysfunctions</u> is based on the specific disorder and can include <u>psychotherapy</u>, <u>sex therapy</u>, <u>pelvic floor physical therapy</u>, and/or pharmacological treatment. Congenital conditions affecting sex are covered separately in “<u>Differences (disorders) of sex development</u>.”




<u>Paraphilic disorders</u> are a group of psychiatric disorders characterized by abnormally intense and persistent sexual interests that manifest as urges, fantasies, or behaviors and involve a nonconsenting individual or cause significant <u>distress</u> or functional impairment in the affected individual. These disorders are distinct from <u>paraphilias</u>, which are also characterized by intense and persistent sexual interests but do not cause significant <u>distress</u> or functional impairment.

---

## Sexual dysfunction

### <u>DSM-5</u> diagnostic criteria for <u>sexual dysfunction</u> [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)




* The symptoms are present for at least 6 months.

* The condition causes clinically significant <u>distress</u> in the individual.

* The dysfunction is not attributable to:

* Another mental disorder (e.g., <u>major depressive disorder</u>, <u>anxiety</u>)

* Severe relationship <u>stress</u>

* Use of substances/medications

* Any medical conditions (e.g., cardiovascular disease, <u>diabetes mellitus</u>)

* Presence of additional condition-specific criteria listed below.





| <u>Sexual dysfunction</u> disorders in the <u>DSM-5</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Conditions |  | <br>Additional condition-specific criteria [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)<br> | Treatment |
| Male sexual dysfunction | Male hypoactive sexual desire disorder | <br>* Persistent or recurrent deficiency or absence of sexual thoughts and desire for <u>sexual activity</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Cognitive-behavioral and <u>psychodynamic therapy</u><br><br>* <u>Sex therapy</u><br><br>* <u>Testosterone</u> replacement therapy<br><br><br> |
| Erectile disorder | <br>* ≥ 1 of the following occur during ≥ 75% of all sexual encounters:<br><br>* Difficulty developing an <u>erection</u><br><br>* Difficulty maintaining an <u>erection</u><br><br>* Reduced rigidity of the <u>erection</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Psychodynamic psychotherapy</u><br><br>* Counseling<br><br>* <u>Sensate focus exercises</u> for <u>performance anxiety</u><br><br>* <u>Group psychotherapy</u><br><br>* Pharmacological treatment: see “<u>Treatment of ED</u>.”<br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Premature ejaculation  [[2]](/library/7XX4z9)<br> | <br><br>* Persistent or recurrent <u>ejaculation</u> within ∼ 1 minute of penetration and before the patient wishes to ejaculate<br><br>* Occurs in ≥ 75% of all sexual encounters<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Psychotherapy</u><br><br>* <u>Cognitive-behavioral therapy</u><br><br>* Pharmacological treatment<br><br>* <u>SSRIs</u> (e.g., <u>paroxetine</u> ) are first-line treatment.<br><br>* Topical <u>anesthetics</u> (e.g., <u>lidocaine</u>-<u>prilocaine</u> spray)  can also be used in combination with <u>SSRIs</u> and <u>psychotherapy</u>.<br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Delayed ejaculation [[3]](/library/HXXKz9)<br> | <br>* ≥ 1 of the following occur during ≥ 75% of all sexual encounters:<br><br>* <u>Delayed ejaculation</u><br><br>* Infrequent or absent <u>ejaculation</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Psychodynamic psychotherapy</u><br><br>* <u>Sensate focus exercises</u><br><br>* <u>Sex therapy</u><br><br><br> |  |
| Female sexual dysfunction | Female sexual interest/arousal disorder | <br>* Absence of or reduction in ≥ 3 of the following:<br><br>* Interest in <u>sexual activity</u><br><br>* Sexual thoughts or fantasies<br><br>* Initiation or participation in <u>sexual activities</u><br><br>* Sexual excitement/pleasure in most (≥ 75%) sexual encounters<br><br>* Sexual arousal to sexual cues<br><br>* Genital or nongenital sexual sensations during most (≥ 75%) sexual encounters<br><br> | <br><br>* Cognitive-behavioral and <u>psychodynamic therapy</u><br><br>* <u>Sex therapy</u><br><br>* Low-dose <u>testosterone</u> and/or vaginal <u>hormone replacement therapy</u> (<u>postmenopausal</u> women)<br><br><br> |
| <br>Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder [[4]](/library/AldRzJ0)<br> | <br>* Persistent or recurrent difficulty with ≥ 1 of the following:<br><br>* Vaginal penetration during sexual intercourse<br><br>* Severe vulvovaginal or <u>pelvic pain</u> during vaginal intercourse or attempted penetration<br><br>* Severe anticipatory <u>anxiety</u> related to vulvovaginal or <u>pelvic pain</u> during attempted vaginal intercourse or attempted penetration<br><br>* Severe tightening of <u>pelvic floor</u> muscles during attempted vaginal penetration (historically referred to as <u>vaginismus</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Pelvic floor physical therapy</u><br><br>* Vaginal dilation<br><br>* <u>Psychotherapy</u><br><br>* Treatment of any causes of <u>dyspareunia in women</u> (e.g., lubricants and moisturizers for vaginal dryness)<br><br><br> |  |
| Female orgasmic disorder | <br>* ≥ 1 of the following occur during ≥ 75% of all sexual encounters:<br><br>* Severely delayed, infrequent, or absent orgasm (e.g., <u>anorgasmia</u>)<br><br>* Reduced intensity of orgasmic sensation<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Psychotherapy</u><br><br>* Education and exercises to facilitate orgasm through self-stimulation<br><br><br> |  |





> [!TIP]
> The most common sexual disorder in men is <u>erectile disorder</u>, followed by <u>premature ejaculation</u>; the two disorders commonly occur concomitantly. In women, the most common disorders are sexual interest/arousal disorder and <u>female orgasmic disorder</u>.




### Contributing factors to consider in diagnosis and treatment




* Factors in <u>patient history</u>,;  e.g., poor body image; , low self-esteem, history of sexual or emotional abuse, stressors, <u>bereavement</u>

* Relationship and partner factors, e.g., partner's sexual and medical health, poor communication, discrepancies in sexual interest and arousal

* Psychiatric comorbidities, e.g., <u>major depressive disorder</u>, <u>anxiety</u>

* Nonpsychiatric conditions and lifestyle factors, e.g., <u>diabetes mellitus</u>, tobacco use, insufficient physical exercise

* Cultural or religious factors, e.g., level of sexual education, negative attitudes toward <u>sexuality</u>

* Penile hypersensitivity and hyperexcitability of the reflex arc (for <u>premature ejaculation</u>)





### Differential diagnoses




* Inadequate sexual stimulation

* Organic conditions

* Endocrinopathy;  (e.g., decreased <u>testosterone</u> levels, <u>diabetes mellitus</u>, <u>hypothyroidism</u>)

* Nerve damage (e.g., damage to the spinal cord due to trauma or <u>pelvic</u> <u>surgery</u>, <u>multiple sclerosis</u>)

* Cardiovascular disease (e.g., <u>ischemia</u> due to <u>atherosclerosis</u>)

* Specific differential diagnoses

* <u>Erectile dysfunction</u> due to organic causes (for <u>erectile disorder</u>)

* <u>Dyspareunia in women</u> due to organic causes (for <u>genito-pelvic pain</u>/penetration syndrome)

* Other psychiatric disorders

* <u>Major depressive disorder</u>

* <u>Anxiety</u>

* Substance and/or medication-induced <u>sexual dysfunction</u>

* Severe disturbance in sexual function that occurs during or soon after substance intoxication, withdrawal, or after exposure to a medication that is capable of causing <u>sexual dysfunction</u>

* Examples: <u>SSRIs</u>, <u>antipsychotics</u>, <u>antihypertensives</u>, <u>opioids</u>, <u>alcohol</u>, <u>cocaine</u>

* Management

* Reduce dose or discontinue medication

* See “<u>Substance-related and addictive disorders</u>” for details regarding the management of specific <u>substance intoxication or withdrawal</u>





References:[[1]](/library/Nta-dm)[[5]](/library/eSYxAo)

## Paraphilic disorders

### Definition




* A group of psychiatric disorders characterized by abnormally intense and persistent sexual interests and desires;  (manifested as urges, fantasies, or behaviors) accompanied by significant <u>distress</u> or functional impairment and/or harm to others
* <u>Paraphilias</u> are variations in sexual preference that may manifest as urges, behaviors, and/or fantasies. <u>Paraphilias</u> are not always pathological, and a <u>paraphilic disorder</u> should only be considered if they interfere negatively with a patient’s life and/or that of others.

* <u>Paraphilias</u> and <u>paraphilic disorders</u> are not inherently criminal offenses, but acting on them may constitute <u>sexual assault</u>, <u>rape</u>, or another crime, especially when nonconsenting individuals are involved.





### Diagnostic criteria (according to <u>DSM-5</u>)




* Presence of abnormally intense and persistent sexual interests occur over a period of at least 6 months as specified by condition below.

* Presence of significant <u>distress</u>, impairment in important areas of functioning (e.g., social, occupational), and/or acts directed against nonconsenting individuals

* Presence of additional condition-specific criteria listed below





| Paraphilic disorders |  |
| --- | --- |
| Condition | Additional disorder-specific criteria |
| Voyeuristic disorder | <br><br>* Persistent and intense sexual arousal caused by observation of an unsuspecting person who is nude, undressing, or engaging in <u>sexual activity</u><br><br>* The patient must be ≥ 18 years of age.<br><br><br> |
| Exhibitionistic disorder | <br>* Persistent and intense sexual arousal caused by exposure of one's genitals to an unsuspecting person<br><br> |
| Frotteuristic disorder | <br>* Persistent and intense sexual arousal caused by touching or rubbing against a nonconsenting person<br><br> |
| Sexual masochism disorder | <br>* Persistent and intense sexual arousal caused by being beaten, bound, humiliated, or made to suffer<br><br> |
| Sexual sadism disorder | <br>* Persistent and intense sexual arousal caused by inflicting <u>pain</u>, suffering, or humiliation on another person<br><br> |
| Pedophilic disorder | <br><br>* Persistent and intense sexual arousal occasioned by prepubescent child or children (≤ 13 years of age)<br><br>* The patient is at least 16 years old and at least 5 years older than the child/children.<br><br><br> |
| Fetishistic disorder | <br><br>* Persistent and intense sexual arousal related to, and a fixation on, nonliving objects (e.g., shoes) or nongenital parts of the body (e.g., feet, <u>hair</u>)<br><br>* Criteria of exclusion: Sexual arousal is limited to sex toys and/or clothing used for <u>crossdressing</u>.<br><br><br> |
| Transvestic disorder | <br><br>* Persistent and intense sexual arousal caused by wearing clothes associated with the opposite <u>gender</u> that cause clinically significant <u>distress</u> and/or functional impairment.<br><br>* <u>Cross-dressing</u> for artistic purposes and in settings where it causes no <u>distress</u> and/or functional impairment to the individual is not a disorder and should not be diagnosed as such.<br><br>* <u>Cross-dressing</u> and <u>transvestic disorder</u> must be distinguished from the practice of <u>transfeminine</u> and <u>transmasculine</u> individuals dressing according to the <u>gender</u> they identify with.<br><br><br> |





### Treatment




* <u>Psychotherapy</u> and <u>cognitive behavioral therapy</u>

* <u>Group therapy</u>

* 12-step program (Sexaholics Anonymous) [[6]](/library/CvcqXe0)

* <u>Social skills training</u>

* Pharmacological treatment to suppress sex drive (e.g., <u>antiandrogens</u>, <u>antidepressants</u> such as <u>SSRIs</u>, <u>mood stabilizers</u>)
